posts.title: Old vs new tax regime: how to choose the right one
posts.description: A plain guide to choosing between the old and new income tax regime in India, with a simple way to compare them using your own deductions.
posts.imageAlt: Valam's Income tax screen comparing the old and new tax regime on a phone

blocks.text: Every salaried person in India now faces the same question each year: old regime or new regime? The new regime has lower rates but almost no deductions. The old regime has higher rates but lets you subtract investments, insurance and loan interest. Which one costs you less depends entirely on your own numbers.
What changes between the two

Think of it as a trade. The new regime is the default and keeps things simple: lower slab rates and a standard deduction for salaried people, but you give up most deductions. The old regime keeps the deductions many people have planned around for years.

items: Section 80C investments such as PPF, ELSS, EPF and life insurance, counted up to ₹1,50,000
Health insurance premiums for you and your parents under 80D
Extra NPS contributions
Interest on a home loan for a house you live in
Interest on an education loan

blocks.text: A simple way to decide

Add up the deductions you would actually claim this year, not the ones you might claim. If the total is small, the new regime almost always wins because its rates are lower. If you have a home loan, full 80C investments and health insurance for your parents, the old regime can still come out ahead.

The only reliable answer is to work out tax both ways with your real income and deductions. Rates and limits change in the Union Budget, so always check the current year's slabs on the income tax portal before you file.
Mistakes to avoid

items: Buying an insurance policy in March only to save tax. A deduction is worth it only if you needed the product anyway.
Forgetting that the regime you pick at work can usually be changed when you file your return.
Ignoring other income such as savings interest, rent or capital gains, which is taxed under both regimes.

blocks.text: Filing with the right form

Once you have chosen, pick the ITR form that matches your income. Salary and one house usually means a simpler form. Capital gains, business income or foreign assets need a more detailed one. Keep Form 16, your bank interest certificates and your investment proofs ready before you start.

posts.title: How chit funds work, and how to find their real return
posts.description: Chit funds explained simply: monthly contributions, the auction, the dividend and the prize, plus how to tell whether your chit is earning or costing you.
posts.imageAlt: A chit fund contribution listed among upcoming bills in the Valam app

blocks.text: Chit funds have helped families across South India save and borrow for generations. A group of people pay a fixed amount every month, and each month one member takes the whole pot. It sounds simple, but whether a chit is good for you depends on when you take the money.
How a chit works

Say 20 members each pay ₹5,000 a month for 20 months. Each month the pot is ₹1,00,000. A registered organiser, often called the foreman, runs the chit and keeps a commission, which by law can be at most 5 percent of the pot.

Each month, members who still need money bid in an auction. The bid is the discount they will accept. If someone bids ₹20,000, they take ₹80,000 minus the commission, and the discount is shared among all members as a dividend, which lowers everyone's next payment.
Early prize or late prize

items: Taking the pot early gives you money when you need it, but you accept a big discount. That works like a loan, and the cost can be high.
Taking the pot late means little or no discount, and you have collected dividends along the way. That works like a savings scheme with a return.
In the middle, it can be close to neutral.

blocks.text: Finding the real return

To judge a chit, compare what you paid in each month with what you received and when. Money received early is worth more than money received late, so a proper comparison uses the timing of every payment, the same way a bank works out an interest rate. That single rate tells you whether your chit acted like a loan at a high cost or a deposit with a good return.
Staying safe

items: Join only chits registered under the Chit Funds Act with a known organiser.
Keep receipts for every contribution and the prize.
Do not put emergency money in a chit. You cannot always get it out when you need it.

posts.title: Avalanche vs snowball: which debt payoff method is right for you?
posts.description: Compare the avalanche and snowball methods for paying off loans and credit cards, with a worked example in rupees and when each one makes sense.
posts.imageAlt: Mathi in the Valam app explaining a debt free date with the avalanche method

blocks.text: If you have more than one loan or card, the order you pay them off matters. Two methods are popular. Both start the same way: pay the minimum or EMI on everything. The difference is where any extra money goes.
The avalanche method

Put every extra rupee on the debt with the highest interest rate. When it is gone, move to the next highest. This saves the most interest and usually makes you debt free sooner. In India that often means clearing a credit card balance at 36 to 42 percent a year first, then a personal loan, then a car loan.
The snowball method

Put every extra rupee on the smallest balance, whatever its rate. When it is gone, roll that payment into the next smallest. You pay a little more interest, but you close accounts faster, and each win keeps you going.
A worked example

Imagine a ₹40,000 card balance at 3.5 percent a month, a ₹1,50,000 personal loan at 14 percent a year and a ₹20,000 loan from a friend with no interest. With ₹5,000 extra a month, the avalanche clears the card first and saves the most interest. The snowball clears the ₹20,000 loan first, which feels great but leaves the expensive card running for longer.
Which should you pick?

items: Pick avalanche if you are motivated by the numbers and want to pay the least.
Pick snowball if you have tried before and given up, and quick wins will help you stick with it.
Either way, stop adding new debt while you pay it off. No method works if the card keeps growing.

posts.title: How to track UPI spending without typing every payment
posts.description: UPI makes paying effortless and tracking hard. Here is how to keep track of small UPI payments using bank SMS, categories and a weekly review.
posts.imageAlt: A month of spending in the Valam Activity calendar

blocks.text: UPI has made paying for tea, autos and groceries a two second job. That is great for convenience and terrible for awareness. Twenty small payments a week rarely feel like much, yet they often add up to more than a big purchase you thought hard about.
Why UPI spending is hard to see

items: Payments are small and frequent, so none of them feels important.
They are spread across several apps and sometimes several bank accounts.
UPI app histories show payees, not categories, so you cannot see where the money went.

blocks.text: Use your bank's SMS alerts

Every UPI payment from your bank account triggers a bank SMS with the amount and often the payee. That makes your SMS inbox the most complete record of your spending. A tracker that reads bank SMS on your phone can turn those alerts into categorised transactions without you typing anything.
Sort it into a few categories

You do not need thirty categories. Food and groceries, transport, shopping, bills and eating out are enough to see the pattern. Fix a category once when it is wrong, and a good tracker remembers it next time.
Review once a week

Pick a fixed time, such as Sunday evening, and spend five minutes looking at the week. Which category grew? Which payments surprised you? One small change a week, like ordering in once less, is easier to keep than a big resolution.

posts.title: Safe to spend: the one number that keeps your budget on track
posts.description: What safe to spend means, how to work it out from income, bills and savings, and why a daily number is easier to follow than a monthly budget.
posts.imageAlt: Mathi answering how much is safe to spend today in the Valam app

blocks.text: A monthly budget is a plan. But in the middle of the month, standing at a shop counter, you need an answer to a simpler question: can I spend this today? Safe to spend turns your whole budget into that one number.
How to work it out

items: Start with the money you have now in your spending accounts.
Subtract every bill, EMI and card payment due before your next payday.
Subtract what you plan to save this month.
Divide what is left by the days until payday.

blocks.text: If you have ₹24,000 left, ₹9,000 of bills before payday, a ₹5,000 savings plan and 20 days to go, you can safely spend ₹500 a day.
Why a daily number works

A big monthly figure feels like plenty in the first week and runs out in the third. A daily number adjusts as you go. Spend less today and tomorrow's number grows. Overspend and it shrinks, before the problem becomes a crisis.
Keep it honest

items: Include irregular bills such as insurance and school fees, spread across the months before they are due.
Use your lowest recent income if your pay changes from month to month.
Do not count money already set aside for goals.

posts.title: How to build a monthly budget that actually works
posts.description: A simple five step method to build a monthly budget you can stick to, with a worked example in rupees.
posts.imageAlt: A budget plan with a daily spending figure, shown next to Valam's Plan screen

blocks.text: Most budgets fail for one reason: they are too strict to live with. A good budget is not a punishment. It is a plan that tells your money where to go before the month begins.
Step 1: Start with what actually comes in
Write down your take home income, the amount that reaches your bank account. If your income changes each month, use the lowest of the last three months. This keeps the plan safe in a weak month.
Step 2: List the bills you cannot skip
Rent, EMIs, insurance, school fees, utilities and minimum card payments come first. Add them up. These are your fixed costs, and they are due whether or not you feel like paying.
Step 3: Pay yourself before you spend

Decide a savings amount and move it on salary day. A common starting point is 20 percent of income, but even 5 percent builds the habit. What matters is that it happens first, not with whatever is left.
Step 4: Give the rest a job
What remains is for food, travel, fun and everything else. Split it into a few categories you can remember. Fewer categories are easier to keep.

items: Needs such as groceries and transport
Wants such as eating out and shopping
A small buffer for surprises

blocks.text: A worked example

Say you take home 50,000 rupees. Fixed bills are 24,000. You save 10,000 first. That leaves 16,000 for everything else, which is about 530 rupees a day. Now every purchase has a clear answer: is it inside the 530, or not?
Step 5: Review weekly, adjust monthly
Look at your spending once a week for five minutes. If a category keeps overflowing, the budget was unrealistic. Change the number, not your self respect.

posts.title: Do a subscription audit and cut recurring costs in one evening
posts.description: Streaming, apps, gym and cloud storage add up quietly. A simple one evening subscription audit to find what you pay for and cancel what you do not use.
posts.imageAlt: Upcoming bills and EMIs listed by Mathi in the Valam app

blocks.text: Subscriptions are designed to be forgotten. A streaming plan, a music app, extra cloud storage, a gym you visit twice a month. Each one is small, and together they can cost more than a weekend trip every month.
Step 1: Find every one
Go through three months of bank and card statements and list anything that repeats. Check your app store subscriptions and UPI autopay mandates too, because those are easy to miss.
Step 2: Price them per year
₹199 a month sounds small. ₹2,388 a year does not. Writing the yearly cost next to each one makes the decision clearer.
Step 3: Keep, downgrade or cancel

items: Keep what you used this week and would miss.
Downgrade plans you use lightly, such as a family plan you use alone.
Cancel anything you have not opened in a month. You can always sign up again.

blocks.text: Step 4: Watch for price rises
Services raise prices quietly. Check your recurring payments every few months and question any that went up.

posts.title: Credit card due dates and interest, explained simply
posts.description: Understand billing cycles, statement dates, minimum due and how interest is charged, so you can avoid late fees and costly interest.
posts.imageAlt: A credit card bill due amount next to upcoming dues in the Valam app

blocks.text: A credit card is a short term loan that is free only if you repay it in full and on time. Knowing four dates and two numbers is enough to use one safely.
The key terms

items: Billing cycle: the period, usually about a month, in which purchases are added to one statement.
Statement date: the day your bill is generated.
Due date: the last day to pay without a late fee, often around 15 to 20 days after the statement.
Total due: everything you owe on the statement.
Minimum due: the smallest payment that avoids a late fee.

blocks.text: Why paying only the minimum is costly

If you pay less than the total due, interest usually applies to the unpaid balance and often to new purchases too, until you clear everything. Card interest is commonly quoted per month and is much higher than most loans. Check your card agreement for the exact rate.
A habit that avoids trouble

items: Pay the total due, not the minimum, whenever you can.
Set a reminder three days before the due date.
Keep your spending below about a third of your limit.
Never withdraw cash on a card, because interest starts immediately.

posts.title: The 24 hour rule: a simple way to stop impulse buying
posts.description: Why waiting 24 hours before a non essential purchase works, how to set your own limit, and how a cooling-off wishlist helps you spend on what you value.
posts.imageAlt: Mathi in the Valam app answering whether a ₹45,000 laptop is affordable this month

blocks.text: Sales, one tap checkout and late night scrolling make impulse buys easy. The 24 hour rule puts a small gap between wanting something and buying it. Most urges fade in that gap. The things you still want after a day are usually worth buying.
How the rule works

items: Pick an amount, such as ₹2,000 or ₹5,000, that feels like a real purchase for you.
For anything above it that is not essential, wait 24 hours.
Write it down somewhere instead of keeping it in a cart.
After a day, decide with a calm head.

blocks.text: Why it works

Impulse buys are driven by feeling, not need. A day lets the feeling pass and lets you ask the useful questions: do I have room for this in my budget? Is it worth more to me than what I am saving for?
Make it stick

items: Delete saved cards from shopping apps so buying takes a little effort.
Unsubscribe from sale emails you do not need.
When you do buy after waiting, enjoy it without guilt. That is the point.

posts.title: A personal finance roadmap: six levels from foundation to independence
posts.description: A step by step money roadmap for India, from tracking spending and an emergency fund to clearing debt, insurance, investing and financial independence.
posts.imageAlt: Valam's Plan screen showing the roadmap level Stability

blocks.text: Money advice often arrives as a long list: invest, insure, save, cut debt, plan for retirement. The hard part is knowing what to do first. A roadmap puts those steps in order, so you always know the next one.
1. Foundation
Know where your money goes. Track spending for a month, list your accounts and debts, and make sure bills are paid on time.
2. Stability
Build a small buffer, even one month of essential costs, and go three months without a missed bill or EMI. Stability means a surprise expense no longer becomes a crisis.
3. Debt control
Clear high interest debt, starting with credit card balances and costly personal loans. Keep EMIs to a comfortable share of your income.
4. Security
Grow your emergency fund to several months of costs, and get adequate term life cover if anyone depends on you, plus health insurance for your family.
5. Growth
Invest regularly for long term goals, such as through monthly SIPs, and give each goal a target and a date.
6. Independence
Your investments can cover your costs, so work becomes a choice. It takes years, and every earlier level is a step towards it.

posts.title: EMI or prepayment: how to pay off a loan faster
posts.description: Learn how loan interest works and when a small extra payment saves the most money.
posts.imageAlt: A debt free date next to Mathi explaining a loan payoff plan in the Valam app

blocks.text: Early in a loan, most of each EMI goes toward interest. That is why extra payments made early have an outsized effect. Understanding this can save you a meaningful sum.
How an EMI is split
Each month, interest is charged on the outstanding balance. The rest of your EMI reduces the principal. As the balance falls, interest falls too, and more of the EMI goes to principal.
Two ways to use extra money

items: Reduce the tenure: keep the same EMI and finish earlier. This usually saves the most interest.
Reduce the EMI: keep the same end date and lower the monthly burden. This helps cash flow but saves less interest.

blocks.text: Which loan to attack first

If you have several loans, the avalanche method targets the highest interest rate first and saves the most money. The snowball method clears the smallest balance first and can feel more motivating. Pick the one you will stick with.
Check before you prepay
Ask your lender about prepayment charges and keep an emergency fund before sending large lump sums. Paying off cheap debt while holding expensive debt is rarely the best use of cash.

posts.title: Why your finance app should work offline and keep data on your phone
posts.description: What happens to your data in a typical money app, and why on-device storage and AI are a safer design.
posts.imageAlt: Valam's Home screen with net worth, stored encrypted on the phone

blocks.text: Your transactions describe how you live: where you shop, what you earn, who you pay and when. That is sensitive information, and it deserves careful handling.
The cloud trade off

Many finance apps upload your data so they can analyse it on their servers. This can be convenient, but it creates a copy of your financial life outside your control. That copy can be breached, shared with partners, or used for advertising.
What local first means

items: Your ledger lives in an encrypted database on your phone.
The app works without internet, so it is fast and reliable.
Intelligence such as categories and coaching runs on the device.
You decide whether anything ever leaves the phone.

blocks.text: Questions to ask any money app

items: Where is my data stored, and who can read it?
Is it encrypted, and who holds the keys?
Does the app contain advertising or analytics trackers?
Can I export and delete my data easily?

posts.title: How to split expenses with friends without the awkwardness
posts.description: Practical tips for tracking shared costs, settling up on time and keeping friendships healthy.
posts.imageAlt: Money owed to you next to Valam's Wealth screen with people and balances

blocks.text: Trips, flats and dinners all create small debts. Left untracked, they turn into resentment. A little structure keeps the money simple and the friendship intact.
Agree the rules early
Decide before the trip whether you split equally or by what each person used. Say it out loud once and it rarely becomes a problem.
Record it the same day
Memory fades quickly. Note who paid and who shared the cost right away, with the amount and a short reason.
Simplify the debts
If A owes B and B owes C, A can sometimes pay C directly. Simplifying reduces the number of payments for everyone.
Settle with confirmation
A settlement is real only when the person receiving the money agrees it arrived. Confirmation avoids the classic argument about whether something was paid.

posts.title: Emergency fund: how much do you really need?
posts.description: A clear way to work out the size of your emergency fund, where to keep it and how to build it step by step.
posts.imageAlt: An emergency fund covering 5.7 months, next to Mathi in the Valam app

blocks.text: An emergency fund is money set aside for surprises such as a medical bill, a job loss or an urgent repair. It keeps one bad month from becoming a debt problem.
A simple rule of thumb

Many planners suggest three to six months of essential expenses. Choose the higher end if your income is irregular or you support dependants. Essentials mean rent, food, EMIs, insurance and utilities, not everything you spend.
Work out your number
If your essentials are 30,000 rupees a month, six months is 1,80,000 rupees. That can look large, so build it in stages.

items: First target: one month of essentials.
Second target: three months.
Final target: six months or your chosen goal.

blocks.text: Where to keep it
Choose safe and easy to reach places such as a savings account or a liquid deposit. The goal is access and safety, not high returns.
Make it automatic
Move a fixed amount on salary day into a separate pot. Treat it like a bill you owe to your future self.
